content: The proposed membership list for the guideline development process was made publicly available for review and comments before being finalized. Members of the External Review Group (ERG) were tasked with peer-reviewing the guidelines, including both updated and new recommendations. This group was carefully selected in consultation with the WHO Steering Committee to ensure a balance in geographical representation and gender. It consisted of 15 peer reviewers from diverse backgrounds, including academia, policy and research institutions, program implementation, community organizations, and representatives of networks for key and vulnerable populations. An independent team of external experts, led by a methodologist and with oversight from the guideline methodologist, conducted systematic reviews of the effects of interventions based on key questions identified for the guidelines. Evidence on values, preferences, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness was also compiled and summarized for each question. Representatives from organizations such as the Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership (GARDP), Unitaid, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) attended the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meetings as observers. These organizations have a longstanding history of collaboration with WHO’s Health and Human Services Department. All members of the GDG, ERG, and other non-WHO staff involved in the guideline development process submitted declarations of interest and confidentiality statements to WHO. These declarations were reviewed, and no conflicts of interest were identified that would preclude any GDG member from fully participating in the guideline development process. Annex 2 provides a detailed summary of these declarations. In December 2013, the first GDG meeting was held to identify and agree on key questions of importance for the guidelines. These questions were framed using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. Following this meeting, a survey of GDG members was conducted to prioritize the selected questions and outcomes based on clinical relevance and importance. PICO questions were prioritized for specific populations, including adults, adolescents, pregnant women, people living with HIV, and populations disproportionately affected by sexually transmitted infections (STIs). In September 2020, the GDG agreed to update treatment recommendations for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis. Updated recommendations were developed for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and syphilis, as well as new recommendations on syphilis testing and partner services. PICO questions were formulated to evaluate whether increased doses in single or dual therapy should be used for gonococcal infections, whether multi-dose doxycycline should replace single-dose azithromycin for chlamydial infections, and whether alternative antibiotics should be used for pregnant women with syphilis instead of benzathine penicillin. The critical outcomes identified for the 2016–2017 guidelines, such as microbiological cure and adverse effects (including maternal and fetal effects), were reused for the new guidelines. Scoping meetings were held in 2021 to assess the need for new recommendations on STI testing and partner services. Based on these meetings, new PICO questions were developed for dual treponemal/non-treponemal rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and syphilis self-testing. Comprehensive literature searches were conducted to gather evidence for the updated recommendations. These searches included systematic reviews, randomized and non-randomized studies, and data on values, preferences, costs, feasibility, acceptability, and equity. The searches covered studies up to August 2023 for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis treatment recommendations, and up to February 2020 for STI partner services. Due to limited data comparing dual treponemal/non-treponemal RDTs with standard laboratory-based serologic tests for syphilis, a modeling study was conducted to provide additional evidence. The evidence was synthesized statistically when possible and assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. The certainty of evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. A virtual GDG meeting was held in November 2022 to develop updated and new recommendations. The GDG reviewed evidence-to-decision frameworks and evidence profiles to make judgments about the effects of treatments. Recommendations were finalized electronically and presented during a follow-up meeting in May 2023. The strength of each recommendation was rated as either strong or conditional based on the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility. Good practice statements were made when the GDG agreed that guidance was necessary but a literature review was not warranted due to unequivocal evidence. Remarks and implementation considerations were added to provide further context for the recommendations. The final guidelines were circulated for feedback in September 2023 and subsequently submitted to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee for approval. Managing conflicts of interest was a key priority throughout the guideline development process. WHO’s guidelines for declarations of interest (DOI) were implemented, and DOI statements were obtained from all GDG and ERG members. Eleven GDG members declared interests, and one member was excluded from discussions related to gonorrhea treatment due to involvement in a related study. Other members were approved for full participation as their declared conflicts were unrelated to the topics under discussion. The updated treatment recommendations apply to adults and adolescents, including pregnant women, people living with HIV, and key populations. For gonococcal infections, WHO recommends ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly as a single dose. If ceftriaxone is unavailable or refused, cefixime 800 mg orally with a test of cure is suggested. For chlamydial infections, multi-dose doxycycline is recommended over single-dose azithromycin. For syphilis in pregnant women, alternative antibiotics may be considered if benzathine penicillin is unavailable.
